question: The European Cloud Sovereignty Framework has introduced a Sovereignty Score for providers of cloud services, aimed at testing the resilience of their services, in case of foreign political interference. In the computation of this Sovereignty Score, it can be noticed that ‘Legal and Jurisdictional Sovereignty’ only accounts for 10 % of the total score1.

This limited weighting stands out as relatively puzzling, considering that it regards the ‘national legal system governing the provider’s operations and contracts’ and the ‘degree of exposure to nonEU laws’. 1.
Can the Commission provide an exhaustive explanation of the weighting used for the overall Sovereignty Score, including why the jurisdictional sovereignty component plays such a minor part in it?

Considering that European cloud providers have benefited comparatively less from the recent expansion of the domestic market2, does the Commission intend to adopt some compensatory incentives giving higher weight to the ‘Legal and Jurisdictional Sovereignty’ factor?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (5.1.2026) The European Cloud Sovereignty Framework1 in its published form summarises the criteria by which cloud solutions will be evaluated in the ongoing competition for Sovereign Cloud under the ‘Cloud III’ Dynamic Purchasing System. Access to the detailed specifications is limited to the participants of that competition pursuant to applicable procurement rules.

Sovereignty Objective 2 ‘Legal & Jurisdictional Sovereignty’ received a weighting that is balanced and comparable to the weighting of the other seven objectives. As stated on page 6 of the document, the weighting of Sovereignty Objective SOV-2 considers relevant safeguards otherwise ensured in the procurement procedure, including minimum requirements, mandatory contractual clauses and technical measures.

The Commission further underlines that while each Sovereignty Objective counts towards a global ‘Sovereignty Score’, a cloud solution must also achieve a certain minimum threshold in each objective. This design ensures a holistic and comprehensive implementation of the sovereign objectives, because insufficient performance in one objective cannot simply be compensated by higher scores in others.
In consequence, the Commission considers all criteria to be appropriately represented in the scoring.
